jq -s '{keys: .}' "$@" > "$out/jwks.json"

# The set published below is EXACTLY the files on this command line, and the
# upload replaces the object outright. Leaving one out is a silent
# de-authorisation with every visible signal green, and per A6.5 it produces no
# prompt symptom either: removals have no measured upper bound, so the dropped
# host keeps working for an unknown period and fails to activate a day later,
# long after anyone connects it to this command. Item 3 runs this once per
# enrolled identity, so guard it every time.
#
# Fetch the live set first, and distinguish the two ways it can be absent: a
# genuine 404 is the first publish and there is nothing to drop; anything else
# is a failed fetch, and treating THAT as an empty set would hide every removal.
live="$out/jwks-live.json"
code=$(curl -sS --max-time 20 -o "$live" -w '%{http_code}' \
  "$ISSUER/.well-known/jwks.json?_=$(date +%s%N)" 2>/dev/null) || code=000
case "$code" in
  200) : ;;
  404) echo "no JWKS published yet at $ISSUER -- treating this as the first publish"
       echo '{"keys":[]}' > "$live" ;;
  *)   echo "could not read the live JWKS (http $code); refusing to replace an object" >&2
       echo "whose current contents are unknown. Nothing has been changed." >&2
       exit 1 ;;
esac
# KO_ALLOW_DROP: space-separated kids this publish is permitted to remove. Empty
# by default, so a removal is never something that just happens.
gargs=(); for k in ${KO_ALLOW_DROP:-}; do gargs+=(--allow-drop "$k"); done
if ! python3 "$here/jwks-publish-guard.py" "$out/jwks.json" "$live" "${gargs[@]}"; then
  echo >&2
  echo "Nothing has been changed. Pass every JWK that should stay published --" >&2
  echo "including the hosts already enrolled -- or set KO_ALLOW_DROP='<kid>...'." >&2
  exit 1
fi

cat > "$out/openid-configuration" <<EOF

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ADMIN side. Run on a machine where `gcloud auth login` is done as the human owner of the
# GCP project holding nix-keyring. NEVER run this on the bare test host.
#
# Creates (idempotently): bucket with a static OIDC issuer under hosts/, WIF pool+provider
# trusting that issuer, KMS key host-key, IAM (decrypt for the pool, encrypt+decrypt for you),
# a KMS canary ciphertext, and a sops-encrypted test file. Writes everything the device
# needs into ./out/ (copy that directory back to the device).
#
# Usage: ./admin-setup.sh out/<host>.jwk.json [more.jwk.json ...]
set -euo pipefail
PROJECT="${PROJECT:-sauyon-dotfiles}"
BUCKET="${BUCKET:-ko-keys-sauyon}"           # bucket names are global; change if taken
LOCATION="${LOCATION:-us}"
POOL="${POOL:-ko-hosts}"
PROVIDER="${PROVIDER:-bucket}"
KEYRING="${KEYRING:-nix-keyring}"
KEY="${KEY:-host-key}"
[ $# -ge 1 ] || { echo "usage: $0 out/<host>.jwk.json [...]" >&2; exit 2; }
for f in "$@"; do [ -s "$f" ] || { echo "missing $f" >&2; exit 2; }; done
out="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)/out"; mkdir -p "$out"

# The admin's gcp-key.json (SA with nix-key only) must NOT be used here: it cannot create
# anything and, if GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS points at it, sops/gcloud silently use it.
unset GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS
gcloud config set project "$PROJECT" >/dev/null
ACCOUNT="$(gcloud config get-value account 2>/dev/null)"
echo "project=$PROJECT account=$ACCOUNT"
gcloud services enable iam.googleapis.com iamcredentials.googleapis.com sts.googleapis.com cloudkms.googleapis.com storage.googleapis.com
PROJECT_NUMBER="$(gcloud projects describe "$PROJECT" --format='value(projectNumber)')"

# --- bucket + static issuer ---------------------------------------------------------------
if ! gcloud storage buckets describe "gs://$BUCKET" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  gcloud storage buckets create "gs://$BUCKET" --location="$LOCATION" --uniform-bucket-level-access
fi
gcloud storage buckets update "gs://$BUCKET" --versioning >/dev/null
PUBLIC=1
if ! gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding "gs://$BUCKET" --member=allUsers --role=roles/storage.objectViewer >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "WARN: could not make bucket public (org policy publicAccessPrevention?). Will upload JWKS to the provider directly instead (--jwk-json-path; max 8 keys, manual rotation)."
  PUBLIC=0
fi
ISSUER="https://storage.googleapis.com/$BUCKET/hosts"
jq -s '{keys: .}' "$@" > "$out/jwks.json"
cat > "$out/openid-configuration" <<EOF
{"issuer":"$ISSUER","jwks_uri":"$ISSUER/.well-known/jwks.json","response_types_supported":["id_token"],"subject_types_supported":["public"],"id_token_signing_alg_values_supported":["ES256","RS256"],"claims_supported":["sub","aud","exp","iat","iss"]}
EOF
gcloud storage cp --content-type=application/json --cache-control='public, max-age=60' "$out/openid-configuration" "gs://$BUCKET/hosts/.well-known/openid-configuration"
gcloud storage cp --content-type=application/json --cache-control='public, max-age=60' "$out/jwks.json" "gs://$BUCKET/hosts/.well-known/jwks.json"
if [ "$PUBLIC" = 1 ]; then
  curl -fsS "$ISSUER/.well-known/openid-configuration" | jq -c . || { echo "discovery doc not publicly fetchable" >&2; exit 1; }
fi

# --- WIF pool + provider --------------------------------------------------------------------
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools describe "$POOL" --location=global >/dev/null 2>&1 || \
  gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create "$POOL" --location=global --display-name="ko dotfiles devices"
AUDIENCE="//iam.googleapis.com/projects/$PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/$POOL/providers/$PROVIDER"
pargs=(--location=global --workload-identity-pool="$POOL" --issuer-uri="$ISSUER"
       --attribute-mapping="google.subject=assertion.sub"
       --attribute-condition='assertion.sub.startsWith("device:")')
[ "$PUBLIC" = 1 ] || pargs+=(--jwk-json-path="$out/jwks.json")
if gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers describe "$PROVIDER" --location=global --workload-identity-pool="$POOL" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers update-oidc "$PROVIDER" "${pargs[@]}"
else
  gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc "$PROVIDER" "${pargs[@]}"
fi

# --- KMS key + IAM ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
KEYRES="projects/$PROJECT/locations/global/keyRings/$KEYRING/cryptoKeys/$KEY"
gcloud kms keys describe "$KEY" --keyring="$KEYRING" --location=global >/dev/null 2>&1 || \
  gcloud kms keys create "$KEY" --keyring="$KEYRING" --location=global --purpose=encryption
gcloud kms keys add-iam-policy-binding "$KEY" --keyring="$KEYRING" --location=global \
  --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/$PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/$POOL/*" \
  --role=roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyDecrypter >/dev/null

  --member="user:$ACCOUNT" --role=roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter >/dev/null

  # needs ADC as the human: gcloud auth application-default login (revoke afterwards, see report A6.3)
  sops --encrypt --gcp-kms "$KEYRES" "$out/test-secrets.plain.yaml" > "$out/test-secrets.yaml" || \
    echo "WARN: sops encrypt failed (run: gcloud auth application-default login; then re-run)"
else
  echo "WARN: sops not installed here; run: nix run nixpkgs#sops -- --encrypt --gcp-kms $KEYRES $out/test-secrets.plain.yaml > $out/test-secrets.yaml"
fi
rm -f "$out/test-secrets.plain.yaml"

cat > "$out/env.sh" <<EOF
PROJECT=$PROJECT
PROJECT_NUMBER=$PROJECT_NUMBER
BUCKET=$BUCKET
ISSUER=$ISSUER
POOL=$POOL
PROVIDER=$PROVIDER
AUDIENCE=$AUDIENCE
KEYRES=$KEYRES
PUBLIC_BUCKET=$PUBLIC
EOF
echo; echo "Done. Copy $out/ back to the device, then run device-test.sh there."
echo "Break-glass hygiene: if you ran 'gcloud auth application-default login' for sops, now run: gcloud auth application-default revoke"

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# Cases for install/wif/jwks-publish-guard.py -- the preflight that stands between
3	# enrolling a host and de-authorising the fleet.
4	#
5	# `admin-setup.sh` builds the published key set with `jq -s '{keys: .}' "$@"` and
6	# uploads exactly that. The set is therefore whatever files happened to be on the
7	# command line: hand it the five new hosts' JWKs and shiori is gone, silently,
8	# with every visible signal green -- jq succeeds, the upload succeeds, the bucket
9	# serves a valid JWKS, and the discovery document still resolves. Item 3 runs
10	# this command once per enrolled identity, which is five more chances to type it
11	# with one file missing.
12	#
13	# The item-2 handoff named this as the thing item 3 multiplies: "admin-setup.sh
14	# *replaces* the key set with exactly what it is handed." `jwks-remove-kid.py`
15	# guards the deliberate removal path. Nothing guarded the replace path, which is
16	# the one nobody thinks of as a removal at all.
17	#
18	# The asymmetry measured in A6.5 decides how this guard has to behave. An
19	# addition is live in ~15 s; a removal has no measured bound and was still
20	# accepted 21.7 h later. So a mistaken drop does NOT lock anyone out promptly --
21	# it quietly leaves the fleet running on keys the published set no longer lists,
22	# and the operator finds out when a host reboots a day later. There is no fast
23	# feedback to catch this, which is exactly why it has to be caught before the
24	# upload rather than after.
25	#
26	#   ./tests/wif-publish-guard.sh
27	#
28	# No network. Every case is a crafted pair of key sets.
29	set -u
30	
31	repo="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
32	prog="$repo/install/wif/jwks-publish-guard.py"
33	
34	fails=0; n=0
35	ok()  { n=$((n+1)); printf 'ok %d - %s\n' "$n" "$1"; }
36	bad() { n=$((n+1)); fails=$((fails+1)); printf 'FAIL %d - %s\n' "$n" "$1"; }
37	
38	work=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT
39	
40	# Every "refuse" case below asserts a non-zero exit, and a program that does not
41	# exist also exits non-zero. Without this gate a missing or unrunnable guard
42	# would show up as a suite that mostly passes -- the refusals "working" for the
43	# one reason that means nothing is being checked at all.
44	if [ ! -f "$prog" ]; then
45	  echo "FAIL 0 - $prog does not exist; every refusal case below would pass vacuously" >&2
46	  echo; echo "0 checks, 1 failed"; exit 1
47	fi
48	if ! python3 "$prog" --selftest >/dev/null 2>&1; then
49	  echo "FAIL 0 - $prog is not runnable (python3 $prog --selftest failed)" >&2
50	  echo; echo "0 checks, 1 failed"; exit 1
51	fi
52	
53	jwk() { printf '{"kty":"EC","crv":"P-256","kid":"%s","x":"x%s","y":"y%s"}' "$1" "$1" "$1"; }
54	set_of() { local out="" k; for k in "$@"; do out="$out${out:+,}$(jwk "$k")"; done; printf '{"keys":[%s]}' "$out"; }
55	
56	# run <name> <proposed json> <live json> <expect ok|refuse> [extra args...]
57	run() {
58	  local name="$1" prop="$2" live="$3" expect="$4"; shift 4
59	  printf '%s' "$prop" > "$work/proposed.json"
60	  printf '%s' "$live" > "$work/live.json"
61	  local err rc
62	  err=$(python3 "$prog" "$work/proposed.json" "$work/live.json" "$@" 2>&1 >/dev/null); rc=$?
63	  if printf '%s' "$err" | grep -qi traceback; then
64	    bad "$name: traceback"$'\n'"      $err"; return
65	  fi
66	  if [ "$expect" = refuse ]; then
67	    if [ "$rc" = 0 ]; then bad "$name: expected a refusal, got exit 0"; else ok "$name"; fi
68	  else
69	    if [ "$rc" = 0 ]; then ok "$name"; else bad "$name: expected exit 0, got $rc"$'\n'"      $err"; fi
70	  fi
71	}
72	
73	# --- the safe shapes ------------------------------------------------------------
74	run "publishing the same set is fine"          "$(set_of A B)" "$(set_of A B)" ok
75	run "adding a key alongside the live ones"     "$(set_of A B C)" "$(set_of A B)" ok
76	run "first publish, nothing live yet"          "$(set_of A)" '{"keys":[]}' ok
77	
78	# --- the footgun this exists for ------------------------------------------------
79	run "dropping a live kid is refused"           "$(set_of B)" "$(set_of A B)" refuse
80	run "dropping every live kid is refused"       "$(set_of C)" "$(set_of A B)" refuse
81	# The realistic shape: enrolling five, forgetting the host already enrolled.
82	run "enrolling new hosts while omitting the incumbent" \
83	    "$(set_of N1 N2 N3 N4 N5)" "$(set_of SHIORI)" refuse
84	
85	# --- a drop is allowed only when it is named ------------------------------------
86	run "a named drop is allowed"                  "$(set_of B)" "$(set_of A B)" ok --allow-drop A
87	run "naming one of two drops is still refused" "$(set_of C)" "$(set_of A B)" refuse --allow-drop A
88	run "naming both drops is allowed"             "$(set_of C)" "$(set_of A B)" ok --allow-drop A --allow-drop B
89	# Naming a kid that is not live means the operator's picture of the bucket is
90	# stale -- the most likely reason being that someone else republished. Refusing
91	# is the cheap way to make them look before a replace.
92	run "naming a drop that is not live is refused" "$(set_of A B)" "$(set_of A B)" refuse --allow-drop GONE
93	
94	# --- malformed input is refused, never published --------------------------------
95	run "a proposed set with no usable key"        '{"keys":[]}' "$(set_of A)" refuse
96	run "a proposed set that is not a JWKS"        '{"nope":1}' "$(set_of A)" refuse
97	run "proposed junk that does not parse"        'not json'   "$(set_of A)" refuse
98	run "a duplicate kid in the proposed set"      "$(set_of A A)" "$(set_of A)" refuse
99	run "an entry with no kid in the proposed set" '{"keys":[{"kty":"EC","crv":"P-256","x":"x","y":"y"}]}' "$(set_of A)" refuse
100	
101	# --- the refusal has to name the kids, or the operator cannot act on it ----------
102	printf '%s' "$(set_of B)" > "$work/proposed.json"
103	printf '%s' "$(set_of A B)" > "$work/live.json"
104	msg=$(python3 "$prog" "$work/proposed.json" "$work/live.json" 2>&1 >/dev/null)
105	if printf '%s' "$msg" | grep -q "A"; then
106	  ok "the refusal names the kid that would be dropped"
107	else
108	  bad "the refusal names the kid that would be dropped"$'\n'"      got: $msg"
109	fi
110	
111	# --- a missing live file is NOT treated as "nothing is published" ----------------
112	# That is the dangerous default: if the fetch failed, an empty live set makes
113	# every drop invisible and the guard waves through exactly the publish it exists
114	# to stop.
115	rm -f "$work/live.json"
116	printf '%s' "$(set_of A)" > "$work/proposed.json"
117	if ! python3 "$prog" "$work/proposed.json" "$work/live.json" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
118	  ok "an unreadable live set is refused, not treated as empty"
119	else
120	  bad "an unreadable live set is refused, not treated as empty"
121	fi
122	
123	echo
124	if [ "$fails" = 0 ]; then echo "$n checks, all good"; else echo "$n checks, $fails failed"; fi
125	[ "$fails" = 0 ]

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# ADMIN side. Run on a machine where `gcloud auth login` is done as the human owner of the
3	# GCP project holding nix-keyring. NEVER run this on the bare test host.
4	#
5	# Creates (idempotently): bucket with a static OIDC issuer under hosts/, WIF pool+provider
6	# trusting that issuer, KMS key host-key, IAM (decrypt for the pool, encrypt+decrypt for you),
7	# a KMS canary ciphertext, and a sops-encrypted test file. Writes everything the device
8	# needs into ./out/ (copy that directory back to the device).
9	#
10	# Usage: ./admin-setup.sh out/<host>.jwk.json [more.jwk.json ...]
11	set -euo pipefail
12	PROJECT="${PROJECT:-sauyon-dotfiles}"
13	BUCKET="${BUCKET:-ko-keys-sauyon}"           # bucket names are global; change if taken
14	LOCATION="${LOCATION:-us}"
15	POOL="${POOL:-ko-hosts}"
16	PROVIDER="${PROVIDER:-bucket}"
17	KEYRING="${KEYRING:-nix-keyring}"
18	KEY="${KEY:-host-key}"
19	[ $# -ge 1 ] || { echo "usage: $0 out/<host>.jwk.json [...]" >&2; exit 2; }
20	for f in "$@"; do [ -s "$f" ] || { echo "missing $f" >&2; exit 2; }; done
21	here="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
22	out="$here/out"; mkdir -p "$out"
23	
24	# The admin's gcp-key.json (SA with nix-key only) must NOT be used here: it cannot create
25	# anything and, if GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS points at it, sops/gcloud silently use it.
26	unset GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS
27	gcloud config set project "$PROJECT" >/dev/null
28	ACCOUNT="$(gcloud config get-value account 2>/dev/null)"
29	echo "project=$PROJECT account=$ACCOUNT"
30	gcloud services enable iam.googleapis.com iamcredentials.googleapis.com sts.googleapis.com cloudkms.googleapis.com storage.googleapis.com
31	PROJECT_NUMBER="$(gcloud projects describe "$PROJECT" --format='value(projectNumber)')"
32	
33	# --- bucket + static issuer ---------------------------------------------------------------
34	if ! gcloud storage buckets describe "gs://$BUCKET" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
35	  gcloud storage buckets create "gs://$BUCKET" --location="$LOCATION" --uniform-bucket-level-access
36	fi
37	gcloud storage buckets update "gs://$BUCKET" --versioning >/dev/null
38	PUBLIC=1
39	if ! gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding "gs://$BUCKET" --member=allUsers --role=roles/storage.objectViewer >/dev/null 2>&1; then
40	  echo "WARN: could not make bucket public (org policy publicAccessPrevention?). Will upload JWKS to the provider directly instead (--jwk-json-path; max 8 keys, manual rotation)."
41	  PUBLIC=0
42	fi
43	ISSUER="https://storage.googleapis.com/$BUCKET/hosts"
44	jq -s '{keys: .}' "$@" > "$out/jwks.json"
45	
46	# The set published below is EXACTLY the files on this command line, and the
47	# upload replaces the object outright. Leaving one out is a silent
48	# de-authorisation with every visible signal green, and per A6.5 it produces no
49	# prompt symptom either: removals have no measured upper bound, so the dropped
50	# host keeps working for an unknown period and fails to activate a day later,
51	# long after anyone connects it to this command. Item 3 runs this once per
52	# enrolled identity, so guard it every time.
53	#
54	# Fetch the live set first, and distinguish the two ways it can be absent: a
55	# genuine 404 is the first publish and there is nothing to drop; anything else
56	# is a failed fetch, and treating THAT as an empty set would hide every removal.
57	live="$out/jwks-live.json"
58	code=$(curl -sS --max-time 20 -o "$live" -w '%{http_code}' \
59	  "$ISSUER/.well-known/jwks.json?_=$(date +%s%N)" 2>/dev/null) || code=000
60	case "$code" in
61	  200) : ;;
62	  404) echo "no JWKS published yet at $ISSUER -- treating this as the first publish"
63	       echo '{"keys":[]}' > "$live" ;;
64	  *)   echo "could not read the live JWKS (http $code); refusing to replace an object" >&2
65	       echo "whose current contents are unknown. Nothing has been changed." >&2
66	       exit 1 ;;
67	esac
68	# KO_ALLOW_DROP: space-separated kids this publish is permitted to remove. Empty
69	# by default, so a removal is never something that just happens.
70	gargs=(); for k in ${KO_ALLOW_DROP:-}; do gargs+=(--allow-drop "$k"); done
71	if ! python3 "$here/jwks-publish-guard.py" "$out/jwks.json" "$live" "${gargs[@]}"; then

       --attribute-mapping="google.subject=assertion.sub"
       --attribute-condition='assertion.sub.startsWith("device:")')
[ "$PUBLIC" = 1 ] || pargs+=(--jwk-json-path="$out/jwks.json")
if gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers describe "$PROVIDER" --location=global --workload-identity-pool="$POOL" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers update-oidc "$PROVIDER" "${pargs[@]}"

fi

KEYRES="projects/$PROJECT/locations/global/keyRings/$KEYRING/cryptoKeys/$KEY"
gcloud kms keys describe "$KEY" --keyring="$KEYRING" --location=global >/dev/null 2>&1 || \
  gcloud kms keys create "$KEY" --keyring="$KEYRING" --location=global --purpose=encryption
gcloud kms keys add-iam-policy-binding "$KEY" --keyring="$KEYRING" --location=global \
  --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/$PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/$POOL/*" \
  --role=roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyDecrypter >/dev/null

  --member="user:$ACCOUNT" --role=roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter >/dev/null

    echo "WARN: sops encrypt failed (run: gcloud auth application-default login; then re-run)"

cat > "$out/env.sh" <<EOF
PROJECT=$PROJECT
PROJECT_NUMBER=$PROJECT_NUMBER
BUCKET=$BUCKET
ISSUER=$ISSUER
POOL=$POOL
PROVIDER=$PROVIDER
AUDIENCE=$AUDIENCE
KEYRES=$KEYRES
PUBLIC_BUCKET=$PUBLIC
EOF
echo; echo "Done. Copy $out/ back to the device, then run device-test.sh there."
echo "Break-glass hygiene: if you ran 'gcloud auth application-default login' for sops, now run: gcloud auth application-default revoke"

lines: # genuine 404 is the first publish and there is nothing to drop; anything else
# is a failed fetch, and treating THAT as an empty set would hide every removal.
live="$out/jwks-live.json"
-code=$(curl -sS --max-time 20 -o "$live" -w '%{http_code}' \
-  "$ISSUER/.well-known/jwks.json?_=$(date +%s%N)" 2>/dev/null) || code=000
-case "$code" in
-  404) echo "no JWKS published yet at $ISSUER -- treating this as the first publish"
-       echo '{"keys":[]}' > "$live" ;;
-  *)   echo "could not read the live JWKS (http $code); refusing to replace an object" >&2
-       echo "whose current contents are unknown. Nothing has been changed." >&2
-       exit 1 ;;
-esac
+if [ "$PUBLIC" = 1 ]; then
+  code=$(curl -sS --max-time 20 -o "$live" -w '%{http_code}' \
+    "$ISSUER/.well-known/jwks.json?_=$(date +%s%N)" 2>/dev/null) || code=000
+  case "$code" in
+    404) echo "no JWKS published yet at $ISSUER -- treating this as the first publish"
+         echo '{"keys":[]}' > "$live" ;;
+    *)   echo "could not read the live JWKS (http $code); refusing to replace an object" >&2
+         echo "whose current contents are unknown. Nothing has been changed." >&2
+         exit 1 ;;
+  esac
+else
+  # On the non-public path the key set lives on the PROVIDER (--jwk-json-path),
+  # not in a fetchable object, so there is nothing to diff over HTTP. The replace
+  # footgun is identical there and this guard does not cover it; read the current
+  # set with `gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers describe` before
+  # re-running. Saying so is better than silently fetching nothing and calling
+  # the publish guarded.
+  echo "WARN: bucket is not public, so the key set is held on the provider and this" >&2
+  echo "      publish is NOT guarded against dropping a kid. Check the provider's" >&2
+  echo "      current key set by hand before continuing." >&2
+  echo '{"keys":[]}' > "$live"
+fi
# KO_ALLOW_DROP: space-separated kids this publish is permitted to remove. Empty
# by default, so a removal is never something that just happens.
gargs=(); for k in ${KO_ALLOW_DROP:-}; do gargs+=(--allow-drop "$k"); done

content.content:
## NO EMAILS

**Never write an email address into anything.** Not into files, commit messages,
docs, notes, handoffs or scratch files — mine, colleagues', or service accounts.
This repo is public, and an address is a durable identifier that spreads: it
leaks the work/personal boundary, it enumerates people, and once written it gets
copied onward.

Refer to an account by its **role** — "the personal Google account", "the work
account", "the project's GCS service agent" — or record the command that
recovers the identity at read time (`gcloud config get-value account`) rather
than pasting its output. Role-based wording is better documentation anyway: "must
be the personal account, not the work one" survives an address change; a pasted
address does not.

If an address seems genuinely load-bearing, ask first.

The exception is the git identity already configured in `home.nix`, which git
requires and which is on every commit regardless.

## Commit and Push Policy

This is a personal dotfiles repo on `master`. When asked to commit and push, do both without asking for confirmation. The global "ask before public communications" rule does not apply here.

## Applying config: use `hms`, not `home-manager switch`

`hms` (defined in `home.nix`, documented in `README.md`) pushes, waits for the
commit's CI run on `forge.ko.ag`, then switches — so the switch is a download of
the closure the in-cluster runner built, not a local compile. Expect it to block
for ten-odd minutes. `hms --local` builds here instead.

It refuses on a dirty tree and on a checkout behind `origin/master`. **Both
refusals are the feature.** CI can only build a pushed commit, so do not route
around them with a bare `home-manager switch` — commit and push, or pass
`--local` deliberately and say that you did.

If a run goes red, `hms` prints the job's `error:` lines; read those rather than
re-running blind. Background on why CI is worth waiting for — and the 600s attic
transfer ceiling that made it unreliable for its first 61 runs — is in
`docs/ci-nix-home.md`.

nix shell nixpkgs#shellcheck -c shellcheck install/wif/admin-setup.sh && echo "shellcheck clean" && ./tests/wif-publish-guard.sh 2>&1 | tail -2 && git add -A install/wif/jwks-publish-guard.py install/wif/admin-setup.sh tests/wif-publish-guard.sh && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
wif: refuse a JWKS replace that would drop a published kid

Item 3 enrolls five more identities, and admin-setup.sh publishes
`jq -s '{keys: .}' "$@"` -- the key set is exactly the files on the
command line, and the upload replaces the object outright. Leave one
out and that host is gone from the trust root with every visible signal
green: jq succeeds, the upload succeeds, the bucket serves a valid
JWKS, discovery still resolves. The item-2 handoff named this as the
thing item 3 multiplies.

What makes it worth a guard rather than a checklist is A6.5's
asymmetry. An addition is live in ~15 s; a removal has no measured
upper bound and was still accepted 21.7 h later. So a mistaken drop
produces no prompt symptom at all -- the fleet keeps running on keys
the published set no longer lists, and the first evidence is a host
failing to activate a day later, by which time nobody connects it to
this command. There is no fast feedback to catch it afterwards, so it
has to be caught before the upload.

jwks-publish-guard.py diffs the proposed set against the live one and
refuses on any unnamed drop. A deliberate removal is still possible,
but it has to be said out loud: --allow-drop <kid>, or KO_ALLOW_DROP in
admin-setup.sh. Naming a kid that is NOT live is also refused -- it
means the operator's picture of the bucket is stale, which is the
moment to look rather than replace.

The refusal that matters most is the unreadable live set. Treating a
failed fetch as "nothing is published" would make every drop invisible
and wave through exactly the publish this exists to stop, so
admin-setup.sh separates a genuine 404 (first publish, nothing to drop)
from any other response (refuse). On the non-public path the key set
lives on the provider and cannot be diffed over HTTP; that is now a
loud warning rather than a silent empty fetch.

17 cases in tests/wif-publish-guard.sh. The suite gates on the guard
existing and self-testing first: every refusal case asserts a non-zero
exit, and a missing program also exits non-zero, so without that gate a
deleted guard would show up as 11 of 17 passing.

Found by shellcheck while wiring it up: admin-setup.sh had no $here,
which this needed, so the guard would have failed to exec and blocked
every publish. Defined it alongside $out.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git log --oneline -1

the guard existing first so a deleted guard cannot pass as working refusals.
EOF

To unblock it I need addresses or ssh config for the four Linux principals and mari, plus a way to reach fujiwara non-interactively — or you run the admin steps. Also still unknown per host: which have TPMs (that decides `tpm-keygen.sh` vs `device-keygen.sh` and `wifTpmHosts`). mari is darwin — files, no TPM, and **two** identities.

**So I built the thing that makes item 3 safe when it does run** — the exact hazard the handoff said item 3 multiplies. `admin-setup.sh` publishes `jq -s '{keys: .}' "$@"`: the key set is precisely the files on the command line, and the upload replaces the object. Enroll five and forget shiori's JWK and it leaves the trust root silently, every signal green.

A checklist wouldn't be enough, because of the asymmetry we measured: additions are live in ~15 s, removals have no bound. A mistaken drop produces **no prompt symptom** — the fleet keeps running on keys the published set no longer lists, and the first evidence is a host failing to activate a day later. There's no catching it afterwards.

`jwks-publish-guard.py` diffs proposed against live and refuses any unnamed drop; deliberate removal needs `--allow-drop <kid>` or `KO_ALLOW_DROP`. Naming a kid that *isn't* live is also refused — that means your picture of the bucket is stale. The refusal that matters most: a failed fetch refuses rather than assuming an empty set, because "assume empty" would hide every drop and wave through exactly what the guard exists to stop.

Two things worth flagging. Shellcheck caught that `admin-setup.sh` had no `$here` — my guard call would have failed to exec and blocked *every* publish. And my first test run was a weak red: `refuse` cases pass vacuously when the program is missing, so the suite now gates on the guard existing and self-testing first.

**Verification:** `wif-publish-guard` 17/17, `wif-sts-classify` 16/16, `wif-keygen` 8/8, `wif-jwks` 16/16, `sops-recipients` 7/7, `wif-tpm` 12 with check 8 the only red (on purpose). Shellcheck clean, Python compiles. Two consecutive clean review rounds over unchanged HEAD `5bef5d2`, all four angles both times. Five commits on `drovr/wif-enroll`, unpushed.

**One thing I deliberately did not do:** add the five hosts to `wifHosts` in `home.nix`. `useWif` gates `sops.environment`, so a host listed there without a device key cannot decrypt at all — that edit comes after each host is enrolled and verified, never before.

content.text:
Tried it — good instinct, but the key is dead, and UniFi wouldn't have unblocked item 3 anyway.

**The UniFi API key in sops doesn't authenticate.** The controller at `10.0.0.1` is up and answering (HTTP responses, not timeouts), but every endpoint returns **401** under both `X-API-KEY` and `Authorization: Bearer`:

```
401  /proxy/network/integration/v1/sites     (both schemes)
401  /proxy/network/api/s/default/stat/sta
401  /api/system
404  :8443/api/s/default/stat/sta            (legacy port not serving)
```

A 401 rather than a 403 means authentication failed, not "integration API disabled". The ciphertext hasn't changed since **2026-05-26** (`840a8ed`), so it looks rotated controller-side without updating sops. **That also means the `unifi` MCP server wired up in `home.nix:1525` is broken** — separate from this task, but worth fixing. I read the key only inside a Python process and never put it in argv or output.

**Local discovery doesn't substitute:**
- shiori is `10.0.10.154/16`, gateway `10.0.0.1` — the whole `10.0.0.0/16` is local.
- DNS is `1.1.1.1` with search domain `sjle.co`, i.e. **no local resolver at all** — that's precisely why the hostnames don't resolve. Querying the gateway directly and mDNS both return nothing for all five names.
- ARP has only `10.0.7.100` (fujiwara), `10.0.7.2`, and two unidentified `10.0.10.x`. The other four principals aren't on the network right now.

**And the binding constraint was never discovery.** Even for the one host I can already address, ssh returns:

```
ssh-oidc: not authenticated — run `ssh sauyon@<host>` interactively once
```

I can't perform an interactive login. So an address for utsuho wouldn't get me onto utsuho, and item 3's device half must run *on* each host.

Three things unblock it, in order of how much they buy:

1. **You run `ssh sauyon@10.0.7.100` once** — that establishes ssh-oidc and gives me fujiwara as the admin host.
2. **Power on / confirm reachability** for utsuho, setsuna, kyuusaku, mari. They're not on the network.
3. **Mint a fresh UniFi API key into sops** — fixes the MCP server regardless of this task.

I can sweep `10.0.7.0/24` and `10.0.10.0/24` for port 22 if you want a host inventory, but it won't tell us *which* box is which without a login — so it wouldn't move item 3.

Next (under two minutes): `! ssh sauyon@10.0.7.100 true` to clear the ssh-oidc gate.

content.content:
# Remote darwin builder (mari)

The Linux boxes (utsuho, setsuna, fujiwara) delegate **aarch64-darwin** builds to
**mari** over Tailscale, since nothing else can build darwin (CI is x86_64-linux
only, and you can't cross-build darwin from Linux).

## Topology / naming gotcha

- The live Mac is the Tailscale node **`mari-1`** (`100.106.204.103`, MagicDNS
  `mari-1.tail1beac.ts.net`). The node literally named `mari` (`100.68.16.116`)
  has been **offline for months** — ignore it.
- The dotfiles config is still `darwinConfigurations.mari` (hostname `mari`);
  that's just the config name. The *builder target* is `mari-1`'s Tailscale IP.
- We pin the **Tailscale IP**, not the MagicDNS name, in `builders`: root's
  resolver on the Linux boxes has no `*.ts.net` (MagicDNS/accept-dns off), and
  the Tailscale IP is stable per node.

## How it's wired

**Client side (Linux), in `system/etc/nix/nix.custom.conf` (→ `system/deploy`):**
```
builders = ssh-ng://sauyon@100.106.204.103 aarch64-darwin /etc/nix/mari-builder-key 4 1 - - <base64 mari-1 host key>
builders-use-substitutes = true
```
The nix **daemon runs as root**, so it's root that SSHes to mari-1, using a
dedicated key at `/etc/nix/mari-builder-key` (sops `mariBuilderKey`, rendered
0600 root by `system/deploy`). The last field pins mari-1's SSH host key.

**Builder side (mari), in `flake.nix` `darwinConfigurations.mari`:**
- `nix.settings.trusted-users = [ "sauyon" ]` — the SSH build user must be a nix

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Device side. Generates a TPM-RESIDENT P-256 device WIF key (report A1 #1, A6.5,
# Part A item 2) and prints its public JWK for the admin machine.
#
# The file this writes is not a private key: it is a TPM key blob, wrapped to a
# primary under this TPM's owner hierarchy. Copy it to another machine and it
# signs nothing. That is the entire upgrade over device-keygen.sh, whose
# ~/.config/ko/wif.pem is a plain P-256 private key that anyone who reads it once
# can use forever, from anywhere, indistinguishably from this host.
#
#   ./install/wif/tpm-keygen.sh [path]     # default: ~/.config/ko/wif-tpm.pem
#
# What it does NOT survive:
#   * a TPM clear (firmware setup, some BIOS updates, `tpm2_clear`) -- the owner
#     seed changes and the blob becomes undecryptable. That is a re-enrolment,
#     not a recovery: run this again and publish the new JWK.
#   * a motherboard swap, for the same reason.
# Both are fine as long as another recipient of secrets.yaml still works, which
# is what the paper key and (until the item 4 gate) nix-key are for.
#
# No PCR policy and no auth value: sops-nix decrypts unattended at activation and
# at boot, so anything that needs a passphrase or a matching boot measurement
# turns a kernel update into a host that cannot read its own secrets.
set -euo pipefail

out="${1:-${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/ko/wif-tpm.pem}"
here="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
repo="$(cd "$here/../.." && pwd)"
host="$(uname -n)"; host="${host%%.*}"
tcti="${TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI:-device:/dev/tpmrm0}"

content.text:
Confirmed — `shiori.jwk.json` is from **my own test run at 15:49 today**, kid `Xqs5Nw…`: neither the revoked kid nor the live one. My test generated a key in a throwaway `$HOME`, wrote its public JWK into the directory the admin is told to collect from, then deleted the private half.

That is the `GKJJEO3B…` failure exactly — an unaccountable key one `admin-setup.sh install/wif/out/*.jwk.json` away from being published. Fixing it test-first:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p = "tests/wif-keygen.sh"
s = open(p).read()

old_run = '''run_keygen() { # run_keygen <home> -> stdout+stderr in $work/log, exit status
  HOME="$1" XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$1/.config" "$prog" >"$work/log" 2>&1
}'''
new_run = '''# KO_OUT_DIR keeps the JWK this writes out of the REPO's install/wif/out/. That
# directory is where the admin is told to collect JWKs from, and a test that
# leaves one there plants an unaccountable public key: the private half lives in
# $work and is deleted on exit, so `admin-setup.sh install/wif/out/*.jwk.json`
# would publish a kid nobody holds. That is the GKJJEO3B... incident, generated
# by the test suite instead of by an experiment.
run_keygen() { # run_keygen <home> -> stdout+stderr in $work/log, exit status
  HOME="$1" XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$1/.config" KO_OUT_DIR="$work/out" "$prog" >"$work/log" 2>&1
}

# Snapshot the real out/ so the last check can prove this suite did not touch it.
repo_out="$repo/install/wif/out"
snapshot() { ls -la --time-style=+%s "$repo_out" 2>/dev/null | sort; }
repo_out_before="$(snapshot)"'''
assert s.count(old_run) == 1
s = s.replace(old_run, new_run)

# check 4 must read the redirected location, not the repo's
old_j = 'jwkfile="$repo/install/wif/out/$(uname -n | cut -d. -f1).jwk.json"'
new_j = 'jwkfile="$work/out/$(uname -n | cut -d. -f1).jwk.json"'
assert s.count(old_j) == 1
s = s.replace(old_j, new_j)

# new final check
old_tail = '''echo
if [ "$fails" = 0 ]; then echo "$n checks, all good"; else echo "$n checks, $fails failed"; fi'''
new_tail = '''# --- 9: this suite must not litter the directory the admin collects from -------
if [ "$(snapshot)" = "$repo_out_before" ]; then
  ok "the suite leaves the repo's install/wif/out/ untouched"
else
  bad "the suite leaves the repo's install/wif/out/ untouched"$'\\n'\\
"      A JWK written here is a public key the admin is told to collect and"$'\\n'\\
"      publish, whose private half this suite deletes on exit. Diff:"$'\\n'\\
"      $(diff <(printf '%s' "$repo_out_before") <(snapshot) | head -5)"
fi

echo
if [ "$fails" = 0 ]; then echo "$n checks, all good"; else echo "$n checks, $fails failed"; fi'''
assert s.count(old_tail) == 1
s = s.replace(old_tail, new_tail)
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("test updated")
PYEOF
./tests/wif-keygen.sh 2>&1 | tail -12

wif: stop the test suite planting a JWK nobody holds the key for

Found while staging fujiwara's enrolment: install/wif/out/ held three
JWKs and only one was real. shiori.jwk.json carried kid
REDACTED -- not the live TPM kid,
not the old revoked file kid, and dated 15:49 today, which is when
tests/wif-keygen.sh ran.

The test generates a key in a throwaway $HOME, and device-keygen.sh
writes its public JWK to $here/out regardless of where the private half
lives. The test then deletes $HOME on exit. What is left is a public key
in the one directory the admin is told to collect from, whose private
half no longer exists anywhere -- and `admin-setup.sh
install/wif/out/*.jwk.json` is the obvious thing to type.

That is the GKJJEO3B... incident reproduced by the test suite: an
unattributed kid in the trust root, which took ~33 h and a human to
clear, and whose removal can never be verified because nobody holds the
key to test it with. A6.5 is about exactly this and my own tests were
manufacturing instances of it.

device-keygen.sh now honours KO_OUT_DIR (default $here/out) and the
suite points it at its temp dir. Check 9 snapshots the real out/ before
and after and fails if the suite touched it, so this cannot come back
quietly -- it was red before this commit for precisely that reason, as
was check 4 once it started reading the redirected path.

The stale JWK is deleted. out/ now holds shiori-tpm and fujiwara-tpm,
both with private halves on their hosts, and jwks-publish-guard.py
confirms publishing exactly those two is safe against the live set.

Also removed the comment claiming writing into the real out/ "is the
real workflow and is left alone". It was mine, from two commits ago, and
it was the reasoning that allowed this.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

content.text:
Three pools, from A1 #5:

| Tier | Issuer prefix | Rights on `host-key` | For |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ko-hosts` | `…/hosts` | **decrypt only** | the home-manager principals |
| `ko-admin` | `…/admin` | **encrypt + decrypt** | the admin workstation, for *editing* dotfiles secrets |
| `ko-ci` | k8s API server | decrypt only if CI needs it, plus signer on `ci-sign-key` | CI |

No pool touches `nix-key`.

**Your instinct is right, and it matters more than it looks.** Because `sub` is attacker-chosen (2b), the tier *is* the entire authorization decision — within a tier every device is one KMS principal. So the tier isn't a label, it's the only access control in the system.

Putting fujiwara's user in `admin` would give **encrypt** on `host-key` to a key sitting on a laptop. Anyone who got that key could *rewrite* every dotfiles secret, not just read them. And since revocation doesn't work, you'd have no timely way to take it back.

`host` keeps the two capabilities separate, which is what the split is for: fujiwara's user needs **decrypt** to activate, and the **encrypt** it exercises when you edit secrets comes from your own gcloud account interactively — not from a device key that lives on disk unattended.

Two supporting reasons:
1. A7's migration gate says "all six principals (seven identities, mari twice) enrolled and activated under `host-key`" — all six as devices, fujiwara among them.
2. Only `hosts/` and `ko-hosts` exist. `admin/` and `ko-admin` have never been created, so `host` is also the only tier deployable today.

So: fujiwara's user enrolls as tier `host`, alongside shiori, and the `admin` tier stays a future thing for editing secrets without an interactive gcloud login.

**hms:** `origin/master` = `89c4429`, 8 commits pushed and built by CI. shiori re-activated — `sops-nix.service` Result=success, 5 secrets materialised through the TPM→STS→`host-key` chain, `wif-tpm` 12 checks with only check 8 red (expected; the revoked kid is now ~t+23 h and still accepted). No token 401 this run.

**fujiwara:** checkout fast-forwarded `c8045f1` → `89c4429`, guard present and self-testing. Its locally modified `flake.lock` survived — I checked first that the incoming range doesn't touch that file, which is why a plain `--ff-only` was safe rather than stashing. I did **not** switch fujiwara; only its checkout moved, which is right, since the guard is a script run from the checkout rather than part of the closure.

**The guard justified itself before ever being used for real.** The first dry-run on fujiwara — with only its own JWK in `out/` — refused:

```
this publish would REMOVE 1 published kid: REDACTED
```

That is exactly the silent de-authorisation of shiori item 3 was walking into, caught against the real bucket state. The cause was mundane and easy to miss: `out/` is gitignored, so shiori's JWK never travelled with the merge. Once staged from the worktree, the dry-run reads **"safe — adds fujiwara, drops nothing."**

**Two things remain yours.** The bucket write is still classifier-denied to me. And I confirmed fujiwara's `~/wif-experiment/out/shiori.jwk.json` holds the **old revoked kid** `01HB4BTt8_…` — never glob that directory into `admin-setup.sh`.

The publish, when you want it:

```
ssh 10.0.7.100 'cd ~/devel/dotfiles && ./install/wif/admin-setup.sh install/wif/out/*.jwk.json'
```

That glob is safe for *that* directory now, and `admin-setup.sh` runs the guard itself before uploading.

Next: run that, then fujiwara goes into `wifHosts` + `wifTpmHosts`, `hms` on fujiwara, and `tests/wif-tpm.sh` there to confirm it decrypts on its own identity.

content.text:
Root cause confirmed, and it's two failures stacked — the script reports the second while the operator hits the first:

1. `.sops.yaml` has only `path_regex: secrets.yaml`, so a file under `install/wif/out/` **matches no creation rule and sops refuses before touching GCP**. `--gcp-kms` on the CLI doesn't bypass it.
2. Only with `--config /dev/null` does it get far enough to hit the *actual* ADC problem.

So the script's warning ("run `gcloud auth application-default login`") misdiagnoses it — and that matters, because A6.3 flags exactly that login as the thing to avoid casually: its refresh token is what Shai-Hulud wave 1 harvested. Writing tests for the parts of `admin-setup.sh` I changed, which have none:

input.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Static contracts for install/wif/admin-setup.sh.
#
# This is the script that publishes the trust root. It cannot be exercised
# offline -- every real path talks to GCS, IAM and KMS -- so these are static
# checks on the invariants that were each established by an incident, and whose
# removal would be silent. A static check is weak evidence that the script
# works and strong evidence that a specific mistake has not come back, which is
# what is wanted here.
#
#   ./tests/wif-admin-setup.sh
#
# No network.
set -u

repo="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
prog="$repo/install/wif/admin-setup.sh"

fails=0; n=0
ok()  { n=$((n+1)); printf 'ok %d - %s\n' "$n" "$1"; }
bad() { n=$((n+1)); fails=$((fails+1)); printf 'FAIL %d - %s\n' "$n" "$1"; }

[ -f "$prog" ] || { echo "FAIL 0 - $prog missing"; echo; echo "0 checks, 1 failed"; exit 1; }
src=$(cat "$prog")

has() { printf '%s' "$src" | grep -q -- "$1"; }

# --- the replace footgun --------------------------------------------------------
# The published set is `jq -s '{keys: .}' "$@"`, so it is exactly the files on the
# command line and the upload replaces the object. Omitting one silently
# de-authorises that host, and per A6.5 removals have no measured upper bound, so
# nothing fails until a day later.
if has 'jwks-publish-guard.py'; then
  ok "the publish runs jwks-publish-guard.py"
else
  bad "the publish runs jwks-publish-guard.py"$'\n'\
"      without it, omitting a JWK silently drops that host from the trust root."
fi

# The guard is worthless if the upload can still happen after it refuses.
guard_line=$(printf '%s' "$src" | grep -n 'jwks-publish-guard.py' | head -1 | cut -d: -f1)
upload_line=$(printf '%s' "$src" | grep -n "storage cp .*jwks.json" | head -1 | cut -d: -f1)
if [ -n "$guard_line" ] && [ -n "$upload_line" ] && [ "$guard_line" -lt "$upload_line" ]; then
  ok "the guard runs BEFORE the jwks.json upload (line $guard_line < $upload_line)"
else
  bad "the guard runs BEFORE the jwks.json upload"$'\n'"      guard=$guard_line upload=$upload_line"
fi

# --- a failed fetch must not read as "nothing is published" ---------------------
# Treating an unreadable live set as empty makes every removal invisible and waves
# through exactly the publish the guard exists to stop. Only a genuine 404 is the
# first publish.
if has '404)' && has 'first publish'; then
  ok "a 404 is treated as the first publish, distinctly from a failed fetch"
else
  bad "a 404 is treated as the first publish, distinctly from a failed fetch"
fi
if printf '%s' "$src" | grep -A2 'could not read the live JWKS' | grep -q 'exit 1'; then
  ok "any other fetch failure refuses instead of assuming an empty live set"
else
  bad "any other fetch failure refuses instead of assuming an empty live set"
fi

# --- sops: two different failures, only one of which is about credentials -------
# .sops.yaml's only creation rule is `path_regex: secrets.yaml`, so encrypting a
# file under install/wif/out/ matches no rule and sops refuses BEFORE it ever
# reaches GCP -- "error loading config: no matching creation rules found".
# Passing --gcp-kms does not bypass that; only --config does. Observed live on
# 2026-09-30.
if printf '%s' "$src" | grep -q 'sops.*--config'; then
  ok "sops is invoked with --config, so a non-matching path is not a creation-rule error"
else
  bad "sops is invoked with --config"$'\n'\
"      Without it, encrypting install/wif/out/<f> dies with \"no matching creation"$'\n'\
"      rules found\" because .sops.yaml only matches secrets.yaml -- before GCP is"$'\n'\
"      ever contacted."
fi

# The warning must not send the operator to an ADC login for a failure that is not
# about credentials. A6.3: the refresh token that login leaves in ~/.config/gcloud
# is what Shai-Hulud wave 1 harvested, and A6.3 requires revoking it afterwards.
# Telling someone to run it unnecessarily has a real cost.
warn=$(printf '%s' "$src" | grep -i 'WARN.*sops' || true)
if printf '%s' "$warn" | grep -q 'application-default login' \
   && ! printf '%s' "$warn" | grep -qi 'creation rule'; then
  bad "the sops warning does not blame ADC for every failure"$'\n'\
"      It names \`gcloud auth application-default login\` unconditionally, but the"$'\n'\
"      failure actually seen was a creation-rule mismatch. A6.3 makes that login"$'\n'\
"      a thing to do deliberately, not on a misdiagnosis."$'\n'\
"      got: $warn"
else
  ok "the sops warning does not blame ADC for every failure"
fi

# --- the admin's restricted key must not be picked up silently ------------------
if has 'unset GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS'; then
  ok "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS is unset before any gcloud call"
else
  bad "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS is unset before any gcloud call"
fi

echo
if [ "$fails" = 0 ]; then echo "$n checks, all good"; else echo "$n checks, $fails failed"; fi
[ "$fails" = 0 ]

fi

# Treating an unreadable live set as empty makes every removal invisible and waves
# through exactly the publish the guard exists to stop. Only a genuine 404 is the
# first publish.

  ok "a 404 is treated as the first publish, distinctly from a failed fetch"
else

# about credentials. A6.3: the refresh token that login leaves in ~/.config/gcloud
# is what Shai-Hulud wave 1 harvested, and A6.3 requires revoking it afterwards.
# Telling someone to run it unnecessarily has a real cost.
warn=$(printf '%s' "$src" | grep -i 'WARN.*sops' || true)

   && ! printf '%s' "$warn" | grep -qi 'creation rule'; then

"      It names \`gcloud auth application-default login\` unconditionally, but the"$'\n'\
"      failure actually seen was a creation-rule mismatch. A6.3 makes that login"$'\n'\
"      a thing to do deliberately, not on a misdiagnosis."$'\n'\
"      got: $warn"
else
  ok "the sops warning does not blame ADC for every failure"
fi

if has 'unset GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS'; then
  ok "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS is unset before any gcloud call"
else
  bad "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS is unset before any gcloud call"
fi

echo
if [ "$fails" = 0 ]; then echo "$n checks, all good"; else echo "$n checks, $fails failed"; fi
[ "$fails" = 0 ]

git fetch origin --quiet; git rebase origin/master 2>&1 | tail -2; git add -A install/wif/admin-setup.sh tests/wif-admin-setup.sh && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
wif: sops in admin-setup needs --config, and the warning misdiagnosed it

Seen live publishing fujiwara's kid on 2026-09-30. The JWKS, provider
and IAM all applied; the run then ended with:

    error loading config: no matching creation rules found
    WARN: sops encrypt failed (run: gcloud auth application-default login; then re-run)

Those two lines are about different things. .sops.yaml has one creation
rule, `path_regex: secrets.yaml`, and the file being encrypted lives
under install/wif/out/, so sops matches no rule and refuses BEFORE it
contacts GCP. Passing --gcp-kms does not bypass it; only --config does.
Reproduced both ways: without --config it is the creation-rule error,
with --config /dev/null it gets as far as a real ADC failure.

So the warning named the second failure while the operator hit the
first. That is not a cosmetic mismatch. A6.3 records that the refresh
token `gcloud auth application-default login` leaves in ~/.config/gcloud
is what Shai-Hulud wave 1 harvested, and that it has to be revoked
afterwards. Sending someone to run it for a config mismatch spends a
real security cost on a misdiagnosis.

Now: --config /dev/null on both the direct call and the not-installed
fallback, stderr captured, and three distinct branches -- creation-rule
(a script bug, says so, says do NOT log in), credentials (says log in
AND revoke, citing A6.3), anything else (prints what sops actually
said). All of them state that only the optional test-secrets file was
skipped, since the parts that matter already applied.

tests/wif-admin-setup.sh is new: static contracts for the script that
publishes the trust root. It cannot run offline -- every real path talks
to GCS, IAM and KMS -- so these check the invariants that were each
established by an incident and whose removal would be silent: the guard
runs, it runs BEFORE the upload (by line number, not by presence), a 404
is distinguished from a failed fetch, sops has --config, the warning
does not blame ADC unconditionally, and GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS
is unset. Checks 5 and 6 were red before this commit; 1-4 and 7 were
green, which is what makes the red meaningful.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

content.text: My mistake — `nix build --print-out-paths` returns multiple outputs (bin, man) and I concatenated them. That's exactly what the `pick` helper in `wif-tpm.sh` exists for:

input.command:
timeout 240 ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=10 10.0.7.100 'export PATH=/nix/var/nix/profiles/default/bin:$HOME/.nix-profile/bin:$PATH
cd ~/devel/dotfiles
pick() { local p; for p in $(nix build --no-link --print-out-paths "$2" 2>/dev/null); do [ -e "$p/$1" ] && { printf "%s" "$p"; return 0; }; done; return 1; }
OSSL_ROOT=$(pick bin/openssl nixpkgs#openssl) || { echo "no openssl"; exit 1; }
PROV=$(pick lib/ossl-modules/tpm2.so nixpkgs#tpm2-openssl) || { echo "no tpm2 provider"; exit 1; }
export KO_OPENSSL="$OSSL_ROOT/bin/openssl" OPENSSL_MODULES="$PROV/lib/ossl-modules" TPM2OPENSSL_TCTI=device:/dev/tpmrm0
ISS=https://storage.googleapis.com/ko-keys-sauyon/hosts
AUD=//iam.googleapis.com/projects/484956590837/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/ko-hosts/providers/bucket
TOK=$(python3 home/scripts/ko-wif-token.py --key ~/.config/ko/wif-tpm.pem --iss "$ISS" --sub "device:fujiwara" --aud "$AUD" 2>/tmp/se) || { echo "SIGN FAILED: $(tail -1 /tmp/se)"; exit 1; }
echo "TPM signed a JWT (${#TOK} chars)"
printf "%s" "$TOK" > /tmp/tok.jwt
CODE=$(curl -sS --max-time 25 -o /tmp/sts.json -w "%{http_code}" https://sts.googleapis.com/v1/token \
  --data-urlencode grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange \
  --data-urlencode "audience=$AUD" --data-urlencode scope=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform \
  --data-urlencode requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token \
  --data-urlencode subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:jwt \
  --data-urlencode "subject_token@/tmp/tok.jwt")
echo "STS: $(python3 install/wif/sts-classify.py "$CODE" /tmp/sts.json)"
if [ "$CODE" = 200 ]; then
  AT=$(python3 -c "import json;print(json.load(open(\"/tmp/sts.json\"))[\"access_token\"])")
  CT=$(cat ~/wif-experiment/out/canary.b64 2>/dev/null)
  if [ -n "$CT" ]; then
    printf "%s" "{\"ciphertext\":\"$CT\"}" > /tmp/req.json
    RC=$(curl -sS --max-time 25 -o /tmp/kms.json -w "%{http_code}" -H @<(echo "Authorization: Bearer $AT") -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -X POST --data @/tmp/req.json "https://cloudkms.googleapis.com/v1/projects/sauyon-dotfiles/locations/global/keyRings/nix-keyring/cryptoKeys/host-key:decrypt")
    echo "KMS decrypt http $RC"
    [ "$RC" = 200 ] && python3 -c "import json,base64;print(\"  canary plaintext:\", base64.b64decode(json.load(open(\"/tmp/kms.json\"))[\"plaintext\"]).decode()[:40])"
  fi
fi
rm -f /tmp/tok.jwt /tmp/sts.json /tmp/req.json /tmp/kms.json /tmp/se' 2>&1 | tail -6

content.text: The existing check is already parameterised by host. The real failure mode for a list edit is adding to `wifTpmHosts` but not `wifHosts` — `useWifTpm = useWif && …`, so the host silently falls back to a file key. Writing that check, then making it red:

input.command: sed -n '36,50p' home.nix
input.description: Read the current wifHosts declarations

input.command:
python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p = "tests/wif-tpm.sh"
s = open(p).read()
old = """echo
if [ "$fails" = 0 ]"""
new = '''# --- every declared TPM host must actually be wired for TPM --------------------
# useWifTpm = useWif && !isDarwin && elem hostname wifTpmHosts. So a host added to
# wifTpmHosts but NOT to wifHosts gets useWifTpm = false and silently signs with
# ~/.config/ko/wif.pem -- a file key it may not even have -- while the list says
# it is a TPM host. Nothing on that host reports the discrepancy; it surfaces as
# an STS 401 at the next activation. Checked here from any host, by evaluating
# each listed host's config rather than trusting the lists to agree.
nixlist() { # nixlist <attr> -> one host per line
  sed -n "s/^ *$1 *= *\\[\\(.*\\)\\];.*/\\1/p" "$repo/home.nix" | tr -d '"' | tr ' ' '\\n' | grep -v '^$'
}
tpm_hosts=$(nixlist wifTpmHosts); wif_hosts=$(nixlist wifHosts)
if [ -z "$tpm_hosts" ]; then
  needed "wifTpmHosts could not be parsed from home.nix" "the TPM host list is readable"
else
  bad_wiring=""
  for h in $tpm_hosts; do
    printf '%s\\n' "$wif_hosts" | grep -qxF "$h" \\
      || bad_wiring="$bad_wiring $h(not-in-wifHosts)"
  done
  if [ -z "$bad_wiring" ]; then
    ok "every host in wifTpmHosts is also in wifHosts ($(echo "$tpm_hosts" | tr '\\n' ' '))"
  else
    bad "every host in wifTpmHosts is also in wifHosts"$'\\n'\\
"     $bad_wiring"$'\\n'\\
"      useWifTpm is gated on useWif, so these evaluate to a FILE key path while"$'\\n'\\
"      the list claims TPM. The host 401s at its next activation."
  fi
fi

echo
if [ "$fails" = 0 ]'''
assert s.count(old) == 1
open(p, "w").write(s.replace(old, new))
print("check added")
PYEOF
python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p = "home.nix"
s = open(p).read()
old = '  wifTpmHosts = [ "shiori" ];'
new = '  wifTpmHosts = [ "shiori" "fujiwara" ];'
assert s.count(old) == 1
open(p, "w").write(s.replace(old, new))

Where things stand:

When it finishes I'll restore the saved lock and run `./tests/wif-tpm.sh` on fujiwara. If the switch fails, fujiwara's `sops-nix` unit is where it'll show, and the fallback is intact: `secrets.yaml` still has `nix-key` as a recipient, so reverting the two list entries restores the old path. I'm not expecting it — I exercised TPM → STS → KMS decrypt on that host before committing the change — but that's the recovery if the activation disagrees with the manual test.

content.text: The not-applicable path reports cleanly. Committing:

input.command:
git add -A tests/wif-tpm.sh && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
wif: the superseded-key checks are per host, not fleet-wide

fujiwara's first run of this suite reported shiori's history. The old
kid was a single pinned constant, so on fujiwara checks 7 and 8
measured 01HB4BTt8... -- shiori's superseded file key -- and check 8's
skip then advised "Keep the old key until this check has gone green,
THEN delete it" about a key fujiwara has never had.

Both halves of that are wrong in the direction that matters. A check
about a different machine passing reads as reassurance about this one,
and advice to preserve a nonexistent key is noise in the one place the
suite is trying to be emphatic -- on shiori that warning is load-bearing,
because deleting wif.pem turns check 8 into a permanent skip and the
suite then says "all good" meaning "we can no longer check".

So the pin is now per host: shiori keeps its kid, anything else defaults
to empty, and empty is reported as "not applicable -- <host> has no
superseded file key (enrolled straight to the TPM), so there is no
predecessor to revoke". A host that HAS a predecessor but lost its pin
still gets the old "no kid pinned" skip, because that one IS a gap.

Verified both paths: on shiori check 8 stays red (its predecessor is
still accepted, now ~t+24 h), and with the pin cleared and the key file
absent the block collapses to one honest not-applicable skip.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git log --oneline -1
